title: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The one septum is, speaking generally, the reverse of the other; the organism, so to speak, is outside the one and inside the other; and in both cases alike, the septum tends to assume the form of a surface of minimal area, as permitted, or as defined, by all the circumstances of the case.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Curvature of septa”. Scope: septa of chambered Foraminifera and chambered cephalopod shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.54

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The geometric predictions are explicit, and public tomography can test them for selected taxa. The causal pressure-side inference remains indirect and confounded by secretion and tissue support.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure septal curvature and attachment boundaries in tomographic shells of Foraminifera and Nautilus, then compare observed surfaces with numerically computed minimum-area surfaces under inferred pressure orientation. Reversed curvature with good minimum-surface fits would support the claim; inconsistent orientation or poor fits would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Preservation and scan resolution can distort thin septa.

Pressure at septum formation is generally absent from museum datasets.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Curvature direction and closeness to a minimal surface are well-defined measurements, and the side the living tissue occupied is known for both groups. The necessary tomographic archives exist but are sparse, so a test would cover a few genera rather than chambered foraminifera and cephalopods at large. Segmentation is routine once scans are in hand, yet assembling a balanced sample would take specialist effort beyond a quick survey.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment septal surfaces from micro-CT of chambered foraminifera and Nautilus, record the sign of curvature relative to the aperture, and compare each septum with the minimal surface spanning the same suture. Support would be outward convexity in foraminifera, outward concavity in Nautilus, and area close to the minimum; a systematic departure toward thicker, non-minimal septa, or curvature unrelated to which side was loaded, would refute the paired claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Minimal-area agreement can be produced by several loading histories, so curvature sign is clearer than the pressure story.

Public volumetric scans of septate foraminifera and nautiloids number in the tens, not a broad taxonomic sample.
